CharDiff: A Diffusion Model with Character-Level Guidance for License Plate Image Restoration

Gyuhwan Park1    Kihyun Na1    Injung Kim2 ††thanks: 1Equal contribution.††thanks: 2Corresponding author.††thanks: G. Park, K. Na, and I. Kim are with the Department of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering, General Graduate School, Handong Global University, Pohang 37554, Republic of Korea (e-mail: park01129@naver.com; kevinna95@gmail.com; ijkim@handong.edu).††thanks: ORCID: G. Park, 0009-0008-7153-5113; K. Na, 0009-0001-3827-5371; I. Kim, 0000-0003-4439-6097.
Abstract

The significance of license plate image restoration goes beyond the preprocessing stage of License Plate Recognition (LPR) systems, as it also serves various purposes, including increasing evidential value, enhancing the clarity of visual interface, and facilitating further utilization of license plate images. We propose a novel diffusion-based framework with character-level guidance, CharDiff, which effectively restores and recognizes severely degraded license plate images captured under realistic conditions. CharDiff leverages fine-grained character-level priors extracted through external segmentation and Optical Character Recognition (OCR) modules tailored for low-quality license plate images. For precise and focused guidance, CharDiff incorporates a novel Character-guided Attention through Region-wise Masking (CHARM) module, which ensures that each character’s guidance is restricted to its own region, thereby avoiding interference with other regions. In experiments, CharDiff significantly outperformed the baseline restoration models in both restoration quality and recognition accuracy, achieving a 28% relative reduction in CER on the Roboflow-LP dataset, compared to the best-performing baseline model. These results indicate that the structured character-guided conditioning effectively enhances the robustness of diffusion-based license plate restoration and recognition in practical deployment scenarios.

Index Terms: 
License Plate Recognition, License Plate Image Restoration, Scene Text Image Super-Resolution, Diffusion Models, Conditional Image Generation, Text Recognition, Masked Cross-Attention

I Introduction

License Plate Recognition (LPR) plays a pivotal role in intelligent transportation systems (ITS), supporting a wide range of applications, including traffic surveillance, automated toll collection, and access control. However, license plate images acquired in real-world environments are often subject to diverse degradations, including low resolution, motion blur, and compression artifacts, which substantially degrade the performance of LPR systems [1, 2].

Previous work has explored image restoration techniques [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] aimed at enhancing LPR performance. However, the significance of license plate image restoration goes beyond the preprocessing stage of LPR systems, as it also serves various purposes, including verifying recognition results, increasing evidential value, improving the visual clarity of advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) interfaces, enhancing user experience, and facilitating the broader utilization of license plate images. Prior studies, including GAN-based super-resolution models [9, 10, 11], and diffusion-based restoration models [12, 13], have demonstrated significant improvements. However, these methods do not effectively exploit the textual information of license plates and, for poor-quality inputs, often synthesize images that either fail to preserve proper character shapes, contain spurious artifacts, or even resembles different characters, as shown in Fig. 1.

To address this challenge, several studies have introduced text-guided restoration techniques into the LPR domain. For instance, recent studies [14, 15, 16, 17] has proposed specialized loss functions that leverage OCR outputs to guide the training process. Although such training-time guidance improves restoration performance to some extent, the model still lacks explicit, inference-time guidance regarding character identities and locations. This limitation can hinder its effectiveness in restoring fine details under severe degradation.

In the STISR field, several recent restoration models have employed conditional diffusion models guided by textual information derived from the input image [18, 19, 20]. However, because they guide the denoising process via global cross-attention, they do not effectively exploit the spatial information of individual characters. As a result, each character-specific prior may not exclusively focus on restoring its corresponding character region, which can lead to interference across other regions. Moreover, a naive application of STISR models to the task of license plate image restoration has the limitation that they do not fully exploit the unique characteristics of license plates.

To overcome these limitations, we propose CharDiff, a novel diffusion-based framework with inference-time character-level guidance, designed to restore and recognize low-quality license plate images. CharDiff integrates fine-grained character-level priors extracted through three modules specifically designed for low-quality license plate images: an external character segmentation module specialized for license plates, an OCR model that is robust to low-quality inputs, and a character encoder that converts individual characters into the corresponding embeddings. The segmentation module leverages the structural format of license plates to reliably identify each character region, even from low-quality images. The OCR model is trained on data containing a large portion of artificially degraded images, making it robust to low-quality inputs. The character encoder extracts more fine-grained character-level features compared to conventional text encoders that produce string-level text embeddings.

Another core component of our framework is the Character-guided Attention through Region-wise Masking (CHARM) module. By applying masked cross-attention, CHARM ensures each character embedding directly guides its corresponding spatial region, while preventing interference with other regions. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first diffusion-based restoration model that leverages character-level guidance through spatially masked cross-attention, overcoming the limitations of conventional models.

We validate our framework on two LPR image datasets: one consists of pairs of high- and low-quality images, where each low-quality image is an artificially degraded version of the corresponding high-quality image, while the other contains only low-quality images captured under realistic conditions without available high-quality counterparts. Experimental results demonstrate that CharDiff significantly improves both image quality and text recognition accuracy compared to the baseline models. For the Roboflow-LP dataset, CharDiff reduced the character error rate (CER) from 11.3% to 8.1% compared to the second-best model, TCDM, achieving a 28.3% relative error reduction. These findings suggest that incorporating character-level priors with spatially guided attention can lead to strong performance in restoring severely degraded images, making CharDiff a promising solution for robust LPR systems in practical scenarios.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    CharDiff: We present a novel diffusion-based framework with character-level guidance tailored for license plate restoration and recognition. CharDiff incorporates fine-grained character-level priors into the restoration process to improve both visual quality and recognition accuracy.

  • •

    CHARM: We present a novel Character-guided Attention through Region-wise Masking (CHARM) module, which directly injects the embeddings of individual characters into their corresponding character regions via cross-attention. This mechanism ensures that each character focuses on its designated region while preventing interference with other regions.

  • •

    Comprehensive Evaluation: We conduct extensive experiments on two license plate datasets, demonstrating improved performance compared to baseline models in both perceptual quality metrics and character-level recognition accuracy.

II Related Work

II-A License Plate Restoration and Recognition

II-A1 Recognition-Only Systems

Traditional LPR systems typically follow a two-stage pipeline: license plate detection followed by character recognition. Most of these systems operate directly on the captured image without any explicit restoration component. Although recent models have evolved from CNN-based architectures [21, 22] to more advanced Transformer-based systems [23], they remain vulnerable to image degradations under realistic imaging environment [24, 25]. Specifically, challenges such as low resolution, motion blur, and sensor noise can severely distort character features, leading to a substantial drop in recognition accuracy [26].

II-A2 Restoration and Recognition Systems

To tackle the challenges posed by low-quality images, numerous studies have incorporated image restoration techniques as a preprocessing step. License plate image restoration models can be broadly categorized depending on whether textual context is leveraged: unconditional restoration and text-guided restoration.

Unconditional restoration models employ general image restoration techniques to enhance low-quality license plate images, without leveraging the textual context of the plates. Early studies utilized CNNs to learn the mapping from low-quality to high-quality images [27, 28, 29]. Given paired low-quality and high-quality images, the model learns to generate high-quality outputs from their low-quality counterparts through supervised learning. Several models adopted generative approaches by incorporating adversarial training objectives [9, 10, 11]. More recent models, such as DiffPlate [12] and LP-Diff [13], apply diffusion models to generate high-quality output images. These methods have demonstrated improved restoration performance, effectively enhancing the visual quality of inputs degraded to a certain extent. However, they fail to fully exploit the unique characteristics of license plate images, limiting their restoration capability for severely degraded inputs.

To overcome the aforementioned limitations, several studies incorporate textual priors. Early work by Zou et al. [30] explored semantic supervision for poor-resolution license plates. More recently, several studies have proposed leveraging textual information by incorporating adversarial frameworks with an OCR-based discriminator or by designing specialized loss functions based on character recognition results [14, 15, 16, 17]. While their approach presents a meaningful step forward, they utilize contextual information only for training and do not directly leverage it during inference. Moreover, they do not explicitly utilize the identity and spatial region of individual characters, which can provide valuable information for image restoration.

II-B Scene Text Image Super-Resolution (STISR)

Among the various applications of image restoration technology, scene-text image super-resolution (STISR) shares many characteristics with license plate restoration. Similar to LPR, STISR aims not only to improve visual quality but also, more importantly, to enhance the legibility of text images for recognition systems. Wang et al. [31] highlighted the discrepancy between synthetic and real-world text degradations and introduced a text-specific architecture, called STRN. STRN incorporates Sequential Residual Blocks (SRBs) combined with LSTMs, and is trained using a boundary-aware loss. While TSRN leverages the unique characteristics of text images in its architecture and training objective, it does not directly exploit the textual content of the input image.

Subsequent studies have more directly leveraged textual context through supervision provided by pre-trained text recognizers. TBSRN [32] incorporated auxiliary OCR-based losses during training. TBSRN employed a text recognizer to provide character-level supervisory signals regarding spatial and semantic information, thereby guiding the super-resolution model during training. However, their method provides text-based guidance only during training and lacks inference-time guidance. Ma et al. introduced inference-time guidance in TPGSR [33], in which the restoration network is guided by a text prior obtained from a recognizer via local, concatenation-based fusion. TATT [34] improved this approach by replacing the local fusion with a Transformer-based module that employs cross-attention to achieve global alignment between the string-level semantic prior and image features.

Recently, diffusion-based restorations leverage textual content during the restoration process. TCDM [19] applies a text-conditional diffusion model to STISR by conditioning the denoising process on a string-level text prior through cross-attention. TCDM leverages textual information from the input image for quality enhancement. However, because it relies on a string-level text prior, it is limited in providing precise guidance on the identities and spatial locations of individual characters. Another recent model, DCDM [20], introduces a dual-diffusion framework to generate more granular, character-level text embeddings. However, since the character embedding guides the image diffusion model through global cross-attention, this model fails to exploit the spatial information of individual characters. As a result, DCDM does not ensure that the guidance of individual characters is focused on the corresponding character regions.

To address the aforementioned challenges in the LPR task, we introduce text-guided diffusion model—demonstrated to be effective in the STISR domain—into the LPR domain, for the first time up to our knowledge, with several enhancements. Specifically, we enhance robustness against image degradation by incorporating an external segmentator that fully leverages the unique characteristics of license plates, along with an OCR model specialized for degraded license plate images. Moreover, by incorporating the CHARM module, CharDiff maximizes the utilization of spatial information across characters to ensure that the prior extracted from each individual character is focused exclusively on restoring its corresponding character region.

III Method

III-A Overview

Figure 2 illustrates the overall process of the CharDiff framework, which aims to restore a low-quality license plate (LP) image by incorporating fine-grained character-level guidance into the diffusion process.

Given a low-quality input image xL​Qx^{LQ}, CharDiff segments individual characters with an external segmentation module customized for license plate images. Then, a robust OCR model recognizes the segmented character images. Subsequently, CharDiff exploits two kinds of contextual information: a sequence of recognized characters 𝐲=(y1,…,yn)\mathbf{y}=(y_{1},...,y_{n}), and their corresponding bounding boxes 𝐁=(B1,…,Bn)\mathbf{B}=(B_{1},...,B_{n}). yiy_{i}’s are converted into the corresponding character embeddings eie_{i}’s through the character encoder. The bounding boxes are converted into binary spatial masks 𝐌=(M1,…,Mn),Mi∈{0,1}W×H\mathbf{M}=(M_{1},...,M_{n}),M_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{W\times H}, where W×HW\times H denotes the feature map size. Mi​[u,v]M_{i}[u,v] is one for (u,v)∈Bi(u,v)\in B_{i} and zero for other elements. The prior from each character consists of the character embedding extracted from the character class and the binary mask derived from its region, i.e., ci=(ei,Mi)c_{i}=(e_{i},M_{i}).

The restoration process leverages a diffusion model with the U-Net architecture. The character-level priors (c1,…,cn)(c_{1},...,c_{n}) are referenced through the CHARM model, which is placed in the middle of the U-Net. In the cross-attention mechanism of the CHARM module, the attention weight for referencing each character’s prior incorporates the spatial mask MiM_{i}, ensuring that the embedding eie_{i} from the ii-th character guides only its corresponding region.

CharDiff combines two types of contextual information: the global image context from the low-quality image xL​Qx^{LQ} and the local context from the character-level priors cic_{i}’s. Therefore, CharDiff is capable of generating high-quality images that remain consistent with the input while accurately preserving the unique features of each character. A detailed explanation of each step is provided in the following subsections.

III-B Diffusion-based Restoration Model

We developed the restoration model based on the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) [35]. DDPM iteratively restores a high-quality image by predicting noise from the intermediate noisy image xtx_{t}. At each timestep tt, the model takes xtx_{t} as input and generates a less noisy image xt−1x_{t-1} by reversing the predicted noise.

In training, xtx_{t} is sampled from the training sample x0x_{0} according to the forward process:

xt=α¯t​x0+1−α¯t​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I).x_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}x_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (1)

The noise predictor, denoted as ϵθ​(⋅)\epsilon_{\theta}(\cdot), predicts the noise ϵ\epsilon from a noisy image xtx_{t} and current timestep tt. Additionally, the noise predictor takes two kinds of contextual information: the low-quality input image xL​Qx^{LQ} that is concatenated with xtx_{t} as xt′=Concat⁡(xt,xL​Q)x_{t}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Concat}(x_{t},x^{LQ}) and a textual context. The output of the noise predictor is an estimation of the forward noise ϵ\epsilon.

The training objective of the noise predictor is as Eq. (3).

ℒcond=𝔼x0,ϵ,t​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(xt′,t,c)‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\text{cond}}=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},\epsilon,t}\left[\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t}^{\prime},t,c)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (2)

The form of the text prior cc can vary in granularity. In this work, we explore three settings:

  • •

    No Text Prior: The model relies solely on the LR image for guidance, i.e., c=∅c=\emptyset.

  • •

    String-Level Text Prior: A single embedding representing the entire text string, i.e., c=e𝐲c=e_{\mathbf{y}}.

  • •

    Character-Level Text Prior (Ours): A set of localized priors, each consisting of a character embedding and a spatial mask, i.e., c={(ei,Mi)}i=1nc=\{(e_{i},M_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}.

Following the strategy of TCDM [19], we inject these text priors cc into the middle block of the U-Net. This design allows the model to incorporate high-level semantic guidance while preserving low-level visual features in the earlier layers.

However, TCDM leverages a text prior through a single, global embedding that is shared across all spatial locations. Such global priors may lack the spatial specificity required for the precise restoration of each character’s shape. This limitation is particularly pronounced in license plate restoration, where accurate reconstruction of individual characters is essential for downstream recognition performance.

In contrast, our character-level prior provides spatially localized guidance through character embeddings and binary masks, with the mechanisms for extraction and injection described in the following sections.

III-C Character-Level Prior

We construct character-level priors from the low-resolution license plate image xL​Qx^{LQ}, where each prior is composed of a semantic embedding and a spatial mask: {(ei,Mi)}i=1n\{(e_{i},M_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}. The extraction process consists of three stages: character segmentation, character recognition, and embedding projection.

(1) Character Segmentation and Mask Generation To localize character regions, we utilize a CRAFT-based text detector [36], fine-tuned on an internal dataset, which is independent of the Roboflow-LP and Dashcam-LP datasets employed for training and evaluation in this study. . The dataset was built by collecting real-world license plate images from the Platesmania platform [37] and manually annotating character-level regions. The model outputs quadrilateral character regions, which are converted into axis-aligned bounding boxes {Bi}\{B_{i}\} through post-processing. For each bounding box, we generate a binary mask Mi∈{0,1}H×WM_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W}, where only the elements inside the region are set to one. These masks are resized to match the resolution of the U-Net feature map used in the CHARM module. The segmentation module is frozen during training.

(2) Character Recognition We crop the segmented character regions and feed them to the OCR module to predict their class labels. We adopt MGP-STR [38] for the OCR module, as it consistently outperforms other recognizers, such as ASTER [39], MORAN [40], and CRNN [41], in preliminary experiments. To enhance robustness to low-quality inputs, we further fine-tuned MGP-STR using low-quality license plate images synthesized by an artificial degradation model. The parameters of the OCR model remain frozen during the training of the diffusion model.

(3) Character Embedding The recognized character labels are one-hot encoded, and then converted into character embeddings {ei}i=1n\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} by a lightweight Transformer encoder. Unlike the previous two modules, the embedding module is trained jointly with the diffusion model, allowing it to learn task-specific representations to guide the restoration process.

Consequently, CharDiff extracts a set of localized priors that encode both the class and spatial location MiM_{i} of each character. These priors are delivered to the CHARM module to enable spatially focused and semantically informed image restoration.

III-D Character-guided Attention through Region-wise Masking (CHARM)

To inject character-level priors into the denoising process, we developed the Character-guided Attention through Region-wise Masking (CHARM) module, a lightweight yet effective mechanism designed to enable spatially localized attention.

The CHARM module combines the character embeddings eie_{i} with the intermediate feature map through masked cross-attention, as shown in Fig. 3.

Feature Preparation Let FlF_{l} denote the input feature map of the CHARM module, where ll is the layer index of the input feature map. We first flatten the spatial dimensions to compute the query vector Q∈ℝC×H​WQ\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times HW} for the cross-attention. Each character embedding ei∈ℝCe_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} is expanded to form key and value tensors Ki,Vi∈ℝC×1K_{i},V_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times 1} via 1D convolution.

Region-masked Cross-Attention For a character ii, we compute attention weights between the query QQ and the key KiK_{i}, applying spatial mask Mi∈{0,1}H×WM_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W}, which is flattened to ℝH​W\mathbb{R}^{HW} during computation. The attention map is computed as:

Ai=softmax​(Mi⊙(Q⊤⋅Ki)d),A_{i}=\text{softmax}\left(\frac{M_{i}\odot(Q^{\top}\cdot K_{i})}{\sqrt{d}}\right), (3)

where MiM_{i} is broadcasted and applied element-wise to suppress attention outside the character region. The attended value hi∈ℝC×H​Wh_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times HW} is then:

hi=Ai⋅Vi,h_{i}=A_{i}\cdot V_{i}, (4)

and reshaped back to ℝC×H×W\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W}. hih_{i}’s are added to the feature map via residual connection as Eq. (5), where the cross-attention layers are shared across all ii’s:

Fl+1←Fl+∑i=0nReshape​(hi).F_{l+1}\leftarrow F_{l}+\sum_{i=0}^{n}\text{Reshape}(h_{i}). (5)

IV Experiments

IV-A Datasets

A practical challenge in license plate image restoration lies in the limited availability of datasets containing paired real high-quality (HQ) and low-quality (LQ) images, which are essential for both training and evaluation. Previous studies have tackled this challenge by synthesizing low-quality samples from real HQ images using artificial degradation pipelines [42, 43] or constructing pseudo-paired datasets by capturing license plates from varying distances to simulate quality variations [44, 13]. In this study, we adopted a hybrid approach, where we trained on pairs of real high-quality and synthetic low-quality images, and evaluated our methods using both synthetic and real low-quality images.

We conducted experiments using two distinct license plate image datasets: Roboflow-LP and Dashcam-LP. Roboflow-LP consists of 4,000 high-quality license plate images from the publicly available Roboflow Universe [45], along with their synthetic low-quality counterparts. The low-quality samples were generated from the high-quality images using an extended version of the degradation pipeline introduced in previous work. Wang et al. [46] introduce a strong degradation pipeline; however, it fails to fully capture the complex visual artifacts produced by in-vehicle cameras. To better reflect real-world conditions, we systematically extended its second-order degradation process. Specifically, we incorporated data augmentation techniques to simulate common challenges with dashcam images, including random perspective transformations to mimic varying viewing angles, random contrast adjustments for lighting and weather variations, and dynamic motion blur to emulate vehicle and camera movement. The top row of Fig. 4 displays several examples of the synthetic low-quality samples in Roboflow-LP. The Roboflow-LP dataset is split into training, validation, and test sets with a ratio of 7:2:1.

Dashcam-LP comprises 10,000 images captured from vehicle dashcams under diverse driving conditions. It includes 9,000 real high-quality images for training and 1,000 real low-quality images for test. The low-quality test samples were independently collected under challenging conditions (e.g., long distances, motion blur) and do not have corresponding high-quality counterparts. Examples of low-quality test images in Dashcam-LP are displayed in the top row of Fig. 5. For training, we synthesized the low-quality counterparts of the training samples using the degradation pipeline used for Roboflow-LP.

We trained two separate models using the training splits of Roboflow-LP and Dashcam-LP, respectively, and evaluated them on the test split of Roboflow-LP and the real low-quality images in the test split of Dashcam-LP. This dual-evaluation setup enables a comprehensive assessment of model performance across both controlled synthetic conditions and challenging real-world scenarios.

IV-B Evaluation Metrics

For evaluation, we assessed both image restoration quality and performance on the downstream task of license plate recognition. For restoration quality, we measured PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on the test set of Roboflow-LP, where ground-truth (GT) high-quality images are available. These three metrics provide a holistic view of restoration fidelity: PSNR captures pixel-level accuracy, SSIM measures structural integrity, and LPIPS quantifies perceptual similarity, where lower scores indicate better quality.

To evaluate recognition performance, we employ two standard metrics: Character Error Rate (CER) and plate-level accuracy. CER measures the normalized Levenshtein distance between predicted and ground-truth strings, whereas plate-level accuracy represents the proportion of license plates that are predicted entirely correctly. These LPR metrics are computed on both synthetic and real-world test sets, enabling an assessment of generalization across in-distribution and naturally degraded conditions. Both the restoration and recognition performances were evaluated on the restored images.

IV-C Baselines

To validate the effectiveness of the proposed model, we conduct a comprehensive comparison against three strong and representative baselines. These baselines were carefully chosen from the closely related fields of STISR and general image restoration. Our evaluation of CharDiff focuses on multiple critical aspects: its performance relative to a general-purpose text-guided model, the impact of text guidance itself, and the effect of guidance granularity within a diffusion framework.

TPGSR

TPGSR [33] is a representative general-purpose STISR model that leverages an internal text prior to guide the restoration process. We include it to evaluate CharDiff’s performance against a model designed for broader scene-text scenarios and to assess its adaptability to the specific challenges posed by license plates. Both the official pretrained model and a version fine-tuned on our license plate datasets are evaluated.

DDPM

We adopt a standard Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) [35] as a key ablation baseline to assess the effectiveness of a diffusion-based approach. In this setup, where the model is conditioned solely on the low-quality image, we can isolate the contributions of our text-based guidance. Our implementation serves as a proxy for recent unconditional diffusion-based LPR models, such as the non-publicly available DiffPlate [12], and is trained from scratch on our LP datasets.

TCDM

TCDM [19], introduced in 2024, is a diffusion-based STISR model that leverages string-level text priors. Including TCDM is crucial for a direct comparison with our method, which employs a different level of text granularity (string-level vs. character-level), thereby testing a key hypothesis of our work. In our evaluation, we consider both the original pretrained version and a variant fine-tuned on our license plate data. We compare CharDiff with these baselines under identical training and evaluation settings to ensure a rigorous and consistent analysis.

We compared CharDiff with these baselines under identical training and evaluation settings to ensure a rigorous and consistent analysis.

IV-D Implementation Details

We implemented CharDiff based on the official DDPM codebase [35]. The diffusion process consists of 1,000 forward steps with a linear noise schedule. The number of steps for restoration was set to 50. We trained the model to minimize the loss function presented in Eq. 2. We employed the AdamW optimizer [47] with a batch size of 64 and a fixed learning rate of 3e-4 for 100k training steps. All input images were resized to 96×48 pixels, which reflects the typical aspect ratio of U.S. license plates. For the baseline models, we followed the implementation details and hyperparameter settings provided in their respective papers. All experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU under identical data splits and evaluation protocols to ensure a fair and consistent comparison.

IV-E Comparison with Baselines

IV-E1 Quantitative Evaluation on the Roboflow-LP dataset

We evaluated CharDiff using both restoration metrics (PSNR, SSIM [48], LPIPS [49]) and recognition metrics (CER and LPR Accuracy), and compared it against baseline models. Table I presents the evaluation results on the Roboflow-LP dataset, whose test set consists of pairs of real HQ and synthetic LQ images. The real HQ images were used as ground truth to compute the restoration metrics. ’FT on LPI’ indicates that the model was fine-tuned on the license plate image dataset, Roboflow-LP, starting from its pretrained weights. DDPM and CharDiff were trained from scratch without any pretraining, using only LPI data.

The proposed model, CharDiff, demonstrated superior performance across all metrics. Compared to the strongest baseline, TCDM (FT), CharDiff improved PSNR by 0.19 dB, SSIM by 0.0076, and LPIPS by 0.0282. In addition, CharDiff outperformed the baseline models in terms of recognition performance. Compared to the second-best model, TCDM (FT), CharDiff reduced the Character Error Rate (CER) from 11.25% to 8.10%, corresponds to an absolute improvement of 3.15 percentage points (%p) and a relative error reduction of 28.0%. It also achieved the highest plate-level LPR accuracy of 69.7%. Given the poor quality the test images (as shown in Fig. 4), these results confirm that the proposed character-level prior is highly effective in restoring global structure—crucial for identity preservation—as well as fine-grained details.

IV-E2 Quantitative Evaluation on the Dashcam-LP dataset)

To evaluate the models’ generalization abilities on authentic and uncontrolled real-world degradations, we evaluated their recognition performance on the Dashcam-LP test set, which comprises real low-quality images without corresponding high-quality counterparts. Table II presents the evaluation results. ‘FT on LPI’ denotes that the model was fine-tuned on the license plate image dataset (Dashcam-LP) starting from its pretrained weights.

Despite being trained solely on Dashcam-LP training set, CharDiff achieved the best performance, demonstrating its robustness to realistic degradations. Compared to TCDM (FT), CharDiff reduced CER from 16.13% to 15.12%. CharDiff also demonstrated the highest LPR Accuracy of 69.65%, which is 5.98%p higher than TCDM (FT), 63.67, These results show that the proposed methods are effective in dealing with the challenging, unseen degradation types found in real-world scenarios.

IV-E3 Qualitative Evaluation

Fig. 4 and 5 display samples in Roboflow-LP and Dashcam-LP, respectively, along with the restoration results produced by the models. All models generated images with improved visual quality. Nevertheless, the baseline models often produce outputs exhibiting severe artifacts, distorted character shapes, and inconsistent character identities. For instance, the second column of Fig.4 shows an example with the ground-truth (GT) label ‘I777B6‘. All baseline models altered some of the characters’ identities (for example, ’I’→\rightarrow’T’, ’7’→\rightarrow’3’ and ’B’→\rightarrow’8’). In the third column, the baseline models incorrectly restored the first character ’K’ as ’M’. These results indicate that the baseline models had difficulty in handling the ambiguity introduced by image degradation.

CharDiff generated license plate images with enhanced visual quality and legibility, while more effectively preserving character identity. The images shown in Fig. 5 demonstrate the difference in restoration quality more clearly.

Moreover, CharDiff exhibited a substantial reduction in restoration errors that damaged or altered character identity compared with the other models. The left five columns of Fig. 4 displays the images that were successfully restored and recognized by CharDiff. The right two columns present failure cases, where the severe degradation of the input image prevented all models, including CharDiff, from accurately restoring it.

IV-F Ablation Study

To assess the contribution of each design choice in CharDiff, we conducted ablation experiments focusing on three core components: (1) the presence of textual priors, (2) the granularity of guidance (string-level vs. character-level), and (3) the masking of cross-attention (w/o masking vs. region-wise masking). All variants are trained from scratch on the synthetic training set and evaluated on both the Roboflow-LP and Dashcam-LP test sets. Tables III and IV present the results for the two datasets, respectively. The results in both tables demonstrate a clear and consistent performance improvement as each component is added. For brevity, we provide a detailed analysis of Table III here. Table IV shows a similar trend, with reduced performance gains in CER.

Effect of Text Priors Removing the textual prior entirely results in a DDPM-based restoration model, which achieves the lowest scores across all metrics. As shown in Table III, the inclusion of even a simple string-level prior substantially improves performance, reducing the CER from 21.18% to 15.39%. These results indicate that textual guidance plays a crucial role in restoring license plate images.

String-level vs. Character-level Prior We then compared the efficacy of the string-level and character-level priors. Replacing the string-level prior with the character-level prior led to a further significant improvement in recognition performance, reducing the CER to 11.87% and increasing LPR accuracy to 62.1%. These results suggest that character-aligned guidance allows for a more precise reconstruction of fine-grained details compared to a global text prior.

Efficacy of Character-level Masking Strategy Finally, applying our character-level masking strategy through the CHARM module yields the most significant improvement in recognition performance. The CHARM module reduced CER to 8.10% and increased LPR accuracy to 69.7%. The character-level masking led to a slight increase in PSNR, while causing a marginal decrease in SSIM. However, the differences in PSNR and SSIM were insignificant.

Meanwhile, the CHARM module resulted in a substantial improvement in perceptual quality (LPIPS) and, more importantly, superior recognition accuracy. This highlights the practical value of guiding the model to focus on spatially distinct regions. The consistent performance gains on the real-world Dashcam-LP dataset (Table IV) further underscore the robustness and generalization benefits of our complete framework.

IV-F1 Attention Visualization

To provide an intuitive understanding of why our character-level prior with masking is so effective, we visualize the internal attention maps of the U-Net’s middle block in Figure 6. The figure contrasts the attention distribution of a model guided by a standard string-level prior with that of our CharDiff model, which uses character-level priors with spatial masking.

The visualization reveals a critical difference. The model with a string-level prior (middle column) exhibits diffuse and scattered attention. The attention for a given character often “leaks” into adjacent regions, causing feature ambiguity between neighboring characters. This interference can lead to the kinds of character confusion and artifacts seen in the qualitative results.

In contrast, the attention maps from CharDiff (right column) are sharp, localized, and precisely confined within each character’s bounding box. Our CHARM module forces the model to focus on one character at a time in its designated region, effectively preventing attention leakage. This spatial disentanglement allows the model to process each character’s features independently and robustly, which directly explains the significant performance gains documented in our ablation study.

V Discussion

In license plate image restoration, both improving the visual quality of images and preserving the original content are crucial. The diffusion-based restoration models employed in our experiments all enhanced visual clarity effectively. However, DDPM, which lacks a text prior, frequently caused distortions in character shapes. By contrast, TPGSR and TCDM, which incorporate text priors, restored character shapes more accurately than DDPM. Our proposed CharDiff outperformed TPGSR and TCDM by leveraging a finer-grained character-level prior.

These findings suggest that incorporating textual priors is effective in guiding the image restoration process, and that the benefits can be further amplified when high-granularity character-level priors are accurately aligned with their corresponding locations.

Image restoration is generally utilized to enhance recognition performance. However, our results indicate that recognition models themselves can also aid the improvement of restoration models, which is consistent with recent research findings [33, 19, 20].

Nevertheless, CharDiff has an inherent limitation in that it is sensitive to the performance of the recognizer—a challenge common to other restoration models that extensively exploit text priors. In this study, we mitigated this issue by employing a specialized segmentation module tailored to the unique characteristics of license plate images and a robust OCR model fine-tuned on low-quality license plate images, thereby improving the reliability of the text prior.

However, in the field of license plate image restoration, where preserving the evidential value of the original footage is essential, a higher level of reliability is required. This issue can be mitigated by presenting restoration results based on multiple recognition candidates alongside the original footage, while leaving the final judgment to human evaluation. In the long term, research is needed to improve the content-preservation capability of restoration models and to reject images that are excessively ambiguous and thus unsuitable for trustworthy restoration.

VI Conclusion

In this study, we proposed CharDiff, a diffusion-based restoration model that effectively restores severely degraded license plate images by leveraging character-level priors. CharDiff extracts character-level priors through a character segmentation module and an OCR model, which are tailored for license plate images, and uses these priors to guide the restoration process of the diffusion model. To achieve this, we developed the CHARM module, which employs masked cross-attention to ensure that each character-specific prior focuses on guiding the restoration of its corresponding character region.

We validated the proposed methods through extensive experiments on two license plate image datasets containing low-quality images. In comparative experiments with three recent restoration and recognition models, CharDiff demonstrated superior performance in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics. Moreover, in terms of recognition accuracy on the RoboFlow-LP dataset, CharDiff reduced the CER from 11.3% (achieved by the second-best model, TCDM) to 8.1%.

These results indicate that contextual information extracted from image content can significantly enhance the performance of image restoration models. In particular, they suggest that injecting fine-grained, localized priors at precisely aligned spatial positions can lead to even greater performance gains.
